title: Devarim: the scouts retold (Deuteronomy 1:22–46)
hookLine: Moses retells an old failure so it won't be repeated
carry: tell it so it won't repeat

lines: BURY IT, OR WALK THROUGH IT.
cards: After a team fails at something big, there's a choice. Bury it, and hope nobody brings it up. Or walk through it step by step: what was decided, what everyone told themselves, where it went wrong.
It's the meeting nobody puts on the calendar gladly. Moses, standing at the Jordan with a new generation, holds it.
He takes the worst moment of the forty years, the twelve scouts and the night the people wept, and tells it again, in detail, to the children of the people who lived it.

teach.b: The path read this story back in Numbers. Twelve scouts go in, ten come back terrified, the people weep all night, and that generation is told it will die in the wilderness.
Now listen to Moses' version, and notice what he changes. In his telling, the idea of scouts starts with the people. You all came to me, he says, and asked to send men ahead to search out the land.
And he admits, the idea pleased me. He doesn't hide behind God's command. He puts his own yes in the story.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE MURMURED IN THEIR TENTS.
teach.b: The land was good, even the scouts said so, but the people murmured in their tents and said God must hate us. And then the part that's easy to forget: after the decree, a group tried to fix it by force.
They marched up into the hill country without God's blessing, and the Amorites chased them, Moses says, the way bees chase. Panic, and then overcorrection. Two mistakes, not one.
The rabbis tied that night of weeping to a date.

teach.h: THE NIGHT OF WEEPING, THE NINTH OF AV.
teach.b: The Mishnah lists it first among the disasters of the ninth of Av, and the Talmud imagines God saying: you wept for nothing that night, so it will become a night of weeping for generations.
And Devarim is read on the Sabbath right before Tisha B'Av.

teach.h: TELL IT SO IT WON'T REPEAT.
teach.b: Moses tells it so it won't be repeated. Honest about his part, honest about both mistakes.

how: The portion Devarim, with Moses' retelling of the scouts, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, and the Mishnah counts the decree on the wilderness generation among the calamities remembered on that fast.

o: the scouts: the men sent ahead

games.q: inside the retelling — tap the pairs.

s: in Deuteronomy, Moses says the idea of scouts pleased him
he puts his own yes into the retelling.
after the decree, the people simply accepted it
some marched into the hill country anyway, and were chased back like bees.
the rabbis link the night of weeping to Tisha B'Av
the Mishnah lists it first among the ninth of Av's disasters.

games.q: you're Moses, retelling the scouts to a new generation forty years later. how do you tell it?
o: leave it out; why open old wounds?
tell it, including your own part and both mistakes.
games.why: he tells it in full: the people asked, the idea pleased me, they murmured, and then they overcorrected and were chased like bees.

practice: Bring to mind a failure you can bear to look at, not the most painful one. Walk through it the way Moses does: where the idea came from, where you said yes, whether you panicked or overcorrected.
Find the one sentence you'd tell a younger person so they wouldn't repeat it.

wordCard.voice: Devarim. Words, and the book where Moses retells even the failures, so the next generation doesn't live them twice.

orig.note: Hebrew: scouts, or spies. Deuteronomy 1:24 uses a verb from the same root: they spied it out.

carryVoice: Your line: tell it so it won't repeat. An honest telling is a gift to whoever comes next. Day four hundred eighty-five, done.
